name: Dusky Green
lede: Dusky Green is a dusky shade of [[green|green]], one of Robert Ridgway's working names built by the plain grammar of modifier plus base color.

sections.title: A modifier, not a new color
sections.body: Dusky Green joins the modifier *dusky* to one of the eleven basic English color words, [[green]] [1][4]. Ridgway's 1912 plate XXXIII, hue 37-double-prime, sets it low on the value scale and low in chroma, LCH lightness 36 and chroma 12 [1][4]. The ISCC-NBS system calls the same block, 122, 'dark greenish gray,' a Delta-E of 6.6 from Ridgway's point [2]. *Dusky* pairs with other base colors in our naming graph too, among them [[dusky-plum]], applying the same darkening, desaturating grammar to a different hue family [1][4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this shade, as photographed, in 1.92% of 23,781 paintings, 457 paintings; within a single canvas it reads as a distinct area in 219 of them [3]. That ranks it more common than 72% of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, found in 2.8% of that century's 1,674 paintings, 2.8 times the expected rate [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, found by lightness rank but under 2% of the visible canvas, in 44% of its 219 appearances [3]. Paul Cezanne is its most devoted painter, using it in 8 of his 50 works here, 7.1 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [3]. The earliest dated appearance is a painting from 1301, 611 years before the name's first documented record in 1912; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a first [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings from Norway, 3.5 times the expected rate, 6 of 120 Norwegian paintings in our archive [3]. In printed English the word peaks in the 1810s, counting every sense of the word [3].
